claim: The prefrontal cortex and hippocampus are crucial for memory-guided decision-making.
source: The prefrontal cortex and hippocampus are crucial for memory-guided decision-making.
evidence: This is a general statement in the abstract that is supported by the experimental findings presented in the manuscript.

claim: Neural activity in the hippocampus exhibits place-cell sequences at multiple timescales, including slow behavioral sequences (~seconds) and fast theta sequences (~100–200 ms) within theta oscillation cycles.
source: Neural activity in the hippocampus exhibits place-cell sequences at multiple timescales, including slow behavioral sequences (~seconds) and fast theta sequences (~100–200 ms) within theta oscillation cycles.
evidence: This claim is supported by the data presented in Figures 1 and 2, showing both behavioral and theta sequences in CA1.

claim: Clear theta sequences were found in prefrontal cortex, nested within its behavioral sequences.
source: We found clear theta sequences in prefrontal cortex, nested within its behavioral sequences.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by data in Figure 2D-F.

claim: In both CA1 and PFC regions, behavioral sequences maintained representations of current choices during navigation.
source: In both regions, behavioral sequences maintained representations of current choices during navigation.
evidence: This claim is supported by the decoding analysis shown in Figure 1H-I.

claim: Hippocampal theta sequences encoded alternatives for deliberation.
source: In contrast, hippocampal theta sequences encoded alternatives for deliberation
evidence: This is supported by the data in Figure 6, showing CA1 theta sequences representing both actual and alternative choices before the choice point.

claim: Hippocampal theta sequences were coordinated with prefrontal theta sequences that predicted upcoming choices.
source: hippocampal theta sequences encoded alternatives for deliberation and were coordinated with prefrontal theta sequences that predicted upcoming choices.
evidence: This is supported by the data in Figure 6J-L showing coordinated CA1-PFC theta sequences.

claim: During error trials, behavioral and theta sequence representations were preserved to guide ongoing behavior.
source: During error trials, these representations were preserved to guide ongoing behavior
evidence: This is supported by the data in Figure 7B-D showing similar behavioral and theta sequences during correct and incorrect trials.

claim: Replay sequences during inter-trial periods were impaired prior to navigation during error trials.
source: whereas replay sequences during inter-trial periods were impaired prior to navigation.
evidence: This is supported by the data in Figure 7F showing that CA1-PFC reactivation strength predicts correct and incorrect responses.

claim: Nine rats learned the spatial working-memory task over eight training sessions in a single day.
source: All subjects learned the task rules over eight training sessions (or epochs; 15–20 mins per sessions) in a single day
evidence: This is a description of the experimental procedure.

claim: Final performance was 92.5 ± 1.8% for inbound and 80.8 ± 2.8% for outbound trials.
source: final performance: 92.5 ± 1.8% for inbound, 80.8 ± 2.8% for outbound, in mean ± SEM
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the behavioral data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Mean ± SEM = 43.9 ± 7.6 CA1 place cells and 29.8 ± 5.6 PFC cells were recorded per session.
source: mean ± SEM = 43.9 ± 7.6 CA1 place cells, 29.8 ± 5.6 PFC cells per session
evidence: This is a quantitative description of the recorded neural data.

claim: 38.4 ± 1.2% of CA1 cells and 23.5 ± 1.3% of PFC cells exhibited trajectory-selective firing during inbound navigation.
source: mean ± SEM = 38.4 ± 1.2% in CA1, 23.5 ± 1.3% in PFC for inbound
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the single-cell analysis.

claim: 35.0 ± 0.7% of CA1 cells and 20.9 ± 0.6% of PFC cells exhibited trajectory-selective firing during outbound navigation.
source: 35.0 ± 0.7% in CA1, 20.9 ± 0.6% in PFC for outbound
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the single-cell analysis.

claim: The decoding accuracy on the center stem significantly increased in CA1 over sessions for both outbound and inbound navigation.
source: the decoding accuracy on the center stem significantly increased in CA1 (p=0.0003 and <1e-4 for outbound and inbound, respectively)
evidence: This is a statistical result from the decoding analysis shown in Figure 1H-I.

claim: The decoding accuracy on the center stem was stable in PFC across sessions for both outbound and inbound navigation.
source: and was stable in PFC across sessions (p's > 0.05 for outbound and inbound, Kruskal-Wallis test with Dunn's post hoc; Figure 1H and I, right)
evidence: This is a statistical result from the decoding analysis shown in Figure 1H-I.

claim: The prevalence of theta sequences in PFC was similar to that in CA1.
source: The prevalence of theta sequences in PFC was similar to that in CA1 (Figure 2G)
evidence: This is supported by the quantitative comparison shown in Figure 2G.

claim: Higher trajectory scores were observed in CA1 compared to PFC.
source: although as expected, higher trajectory scores (suggesting more reliable timing of sequences) were observed in CA1 compared to PFC (Figure 2H).
evidence: This is supported by the quantitative comparison shown in Figure 2H.

claim: The trajectory scores and slopes in both CA1 and PFC increased over learning.
source: Furthermore, the trajectory scores and slopes (sequence speed) in both regions increased over learning (Figure 2H and I).
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 2H-I.

claim: Approximately 70% of CA1 and 60% of PFC theta sequences were forward sequences.
source: the majority of CA1 (~70%) and PFC (~60%) theta sequences successively represented past, present, and future locations within each theta cycle (i.e. forward sequences; Figure 2J and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A–C)
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 2J and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A–C.

claim: Theta sequences occurred at a velocity approximately 4–15 times faster than an animal's true running speed.
source: at a velocity approximately 4–15 times faster than an animal's true running speed (Figure 2I).
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 2I.

claim: Positions behind the actual location of the animal were decoded with higher probability during inbound than outbound navigation in both CA1 and PFC.
source: We found that the positions behind the actual location of the animal were decoded with higher probability during inbound than outbound navigation in both CA1 and PFC, (Figure 3A–D)
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 3A-D.

claim: Forward sequences in both CA1 and PFC started farther behind the actual position of the animal during inbound navigation.
source: forward sequences in both CA1 and PFC started farther behind the actual position of the animal during inbound navigation
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 3E-F.

claim: Forward sequences in both CA1 and PFC ended farther ahead of the animal during outbound navigation.
source: whereas they ended farther ahead of the animal during outbound navigation (Figure 3E and F).
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 3E-F.

claim: Working-memory-guided outbound navigation was associated with fields with a more extended initial tail compared to inbound travel for both CA1 and PFC.
source: working-memory-guided outbound navigation was associated with fields with a more extended initial tail compared to inbound travel for both CA1 and PFC (Figure 4A–C).
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 4A-C.

claim: The effect of extended initial tail was stronger for trajectory-selective than non-selective cells in both CA1 and PFC.
source: This effect was also stronger for trajectory-selective than non-selective cells in both regions (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Similar slopes of theta phase precession were observed for inbound and outbound navigation in both CA1 and PFC.
source: However, similar slopes of theta phase precession were observed for inbound and outbound navigation in both regions (Figure 4G and H)
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 4G-H.

claim: 53.4% of theta-modulated cells in PFC fired in cycle skipping during inbound navigation.
source: Inbound: 53.4%, 95 out of 178
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the cycle skipping analysis.

claim: 49.7% of theta-modulated cells in PFC fired in cycle skipping during outbound navigation.
source: outbound: 49.7%, 91 out of 183
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the cycle skipping analysis.

claim: Before the choice point, CA1 theta sequences serially encoded both alternative trajectories.
source: Before the CP (corresponding to periods on the center stem for outbound navigation; Figure 6B), CA1 theta sequences serially encoded both alternative trajectories (Figure 6C and G and Figure 6—figure supplements 1–2; Video 1).
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 6C, G and supplementary figures.

claim: Before the choice point, PFC theta sequences preferentially encoded the animal's current choice.
source: In contrast, PFC theta sequences preferentially encoded the animal's current choice (Figure 6E and G and Figure 6—figure supplements 1–2).
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 6E, G and supplementary figures.

claim: After the choice point, both CA1 and PFC theta sequences preferentially encoded the animal's current choice.
source: After the choice was made (i.e., after CP; Figure 6B), as expected, both CA1 and PFC theta sequences preferentially encoded the animal's current choice as the animal's ran down the track toward reward (Figure 6D, F and G and Figure 6—figure supplements 1–2).
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 6D, F, G and supplementary figures.

claim: Upcoming choice was decoded by PFC theta sequences well above chance before the choice point.
source: upcoming choice was decoded by PFC theta sequences well above chance before the CP
evidence: This is supported by the trial-by-trial prediction analysis shown in Figure 6H-I.

claim: CA1 theta sequences encoded actual and alternative available paths equivalently before the choice point.
source: whereas CA1 theta sequences encoded actual and alternative available paths equivalently before the CP (Figure 6H and I).
evidence: This is supported by the trial-by-trial prediction analysis shown in Figure 6H-I.

claim: 10.53 ± 1.42% of outbound theta sequences and 11.17 ± 1.52% of inbound theta sequences were synchronous CA1 and PFC theta sequences.
source: mean ± SEM = 10.53 ± 1.42%, and 11.17 ± 1.52% out of significant sequences for outbound and inbound, respectively
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the analysis of synchronous sequences.

claim: When CA1 theta sequences represented the actual choice, PFC sequences were also significantly biased to the actual choice.
source: Among these synchronous sequence events, when CA1 theta sequences represented the actual choice, PFC sequences were also significantly biased to the actual choice
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 6L.

claim: Coherent CA1-PFC representation was not observed when CA1 theta sequences represented the alternative choice.
source: whereas this coherent CA1-PFC representation was not observed when CA1 theta sequences represented the alternative choice (Figure 6L).
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 6L.

claim: Sequential firing at the behavioral timescale during incorrect trials was similar to that during correct trials.
source: We found that sequential firing that occurred at the behavioral timescale during incorrect trials was similar to that during correct trials (Figure 7B)
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: The decoding accuracy for the chosen side was comparable for correct and incorrect trials.
source: and the decoding accuracy for the chosen side was comparable for correct and incorrect trials (Figure 7C
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 7C.

claim: CA1 and PFC theta-sequence prediction of upcoming choice was similar for correct and incorrect trials.
source: Furthermore, CA1 and PFC theta-sequence prediction of upcoming choice was also similar for correct and incorrect trials (Figure 7D).
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 7D.

claim: Correct versus incorrect trials did not differ in running speed and theta power.
source: Correct versus incorrect trials did not differ in running speed and theta power (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A–B).
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1A-B.

claim: CA1-PFC theta coherence was similar between correct versus incorrect trials.
source: CA1-PFC theta coherence and the strength of single-cell phase-locking to theta oscillations during navigation, which have been proposed to support spatial working memory (Benchenane et al., 2010; Gordon, 2011; Jones and Wilson, 2005b; Sigurdsson et al., 2010), were also similar between correct versus incorrect trials (Figure 7—figure supplement 1C–L).
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1C-L.

claim: The strength of single-cell phase-locking to theta oscillations during navigation was similar between correct versus incorrect trials.
source: CA1-PFC theta coherence and the strength of single-cell phase-locking to theta oscillations during navigation, which have been proposed to support spatial working memory (Benchenane et al., 2010; Gordon, 2011; Jones and Wilson, 2005b; Sigurdsson et al., 2010), were also similar between correct versus incorrect trials (Figure 7—figure supplement 1C–L).
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1C-L.

claim: CA1-PFC reactivation strength for actual versus alternative choices could predict correct and incorrect responses significantly better than chance.
source: using CA1-PFC reactivation strength for actual versus alternative choices preceding the correct and incorrect trials (see Materials and methods), we could predict correct and incorrect responses significantly better than chance (Figure 7F)
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 7F.

claim: The W-maze spatial alternation task is known to require both the hippocampus and PFC for learning.
source: This task is known to require both the hippocampus and PFC for learning (Fernández-Ruiz et al., 2019; Jadhav et al., 2012; Kim and Frank, 2009; Maharjan et al., 2018)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The W-maze spatial alternation task involves memory-guided decision-making.
source: and involves memory-guided decision-making (Jadhav et al., 2016; Shin et al., 2019; Yu and Frank, 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Neurons in the prefrontal cortex and posterior parietal cortex can exhibit persistent activity over seconds throughout retention intervals for maintenance of decision-related information.
source: Early classic work showed that during tasks involving sustained attention or decision-making, neurons in the prefrontal cortex (PFC) and the posterior parietal cortex (PPC) can exhibit persistent activity over seconds throughout retention intervals for maintenance of decision-related information (Fuster, 2015; Goldman-Rakic, 1995; Miller et al., 2018; Sreenivasan and D'Esposito, 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Heterogenous activity patterns comprising sequences of neuronal activation that span entire task periods have emerged as a common coding scheme in many brain regions, including PFC, hippocampus, PPC, and striatum.
source: At the ensemble level, heterogenous activity patterns comprising sequences of neuronal activation that span entire task periods have emerged as a common coding scheme in many brain regions, including PFC (Baeg et al., 2003; Fujisawa et al., 2008; Ito et al., 2015), hippocampus (Ito et al., 2015; Pastalkova et al., 2008), PPC (Crowe et al., 2010; Harvey et al., 2012), and striatum (Bakhurin et al., 2016; Barnes et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Population activity in prefrontal, parietal, orbitofrontal cortices, and hippocampus can change in an abrupt, coordinated, and transient manner in support of flexible decisions.
source: In many brain areas, such as prefrontal, parietal, orbitofrontal cortices, and hippocampus, population activity can change in an abrupt, coordinated, and transient manner in support of flexible decisions (Bernacchia et al., 2011; Durstewitz et al., 2010; Johnson and Redish, 2007; Karlsson et al., 2012; Latimer et al., 2015; Lundqvist et al., 2016; Rich and Wallis, 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Discrete transient bursts of gamma and beta oscillations in PFC have been shown to increase with working-memory load during delays.
source: For example, discrete transient bursts of gamma and beta oscillations in PFC have been shown to increase with working-memory load during delays (Lundqvist et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Hippocampal theta sequences provide time-compressed ensemble representations of spatial paths within single cycles of theta oscillations during active navigation.
source: Hippocampal theta sequences provide time-compressed ensemble representations of spatial paths within single cycles of theta oscillations (6–12 Hz) during active navigation, which reflect a candidate neural mechanism for planning at decision time (Johnson and Redish, 2007; Kay et al., 2020; Papale et al., 2016; Pezzulo et al., 2019; Zheng et al., 2020; Zielinski et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Replay sequences are observed in the hippocampus during individual sharp-wave ripples during pauses in exploration.
source: Further, during pauses in exploration, replay sequences are observed in the hippocampus during individual sharp-wave ripples (SWRs; Carr et al., 2011)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Hippocampal replay sequences are known to interact with PFC to reactivate past and future trajectories on the temporal scale of 100–200 ms during memory-guided decisions.
source: and are known to interact with PFC to reactivate past and future trajectories on the temporal scale of 100–200 ms during memory-guided decisions (Shin et al., 2019; Tang and Jadhav, 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Disruption of fast sequences in the hippocampus, while leaving behavioral-timescale spatial representations intact, can impair navigation decisions.
source: Disruption of fast sequences in the hippocampus, while leaving behavioral-timescale spatial representations intact, can impair navigation decisions (Fernández-Ruiz et al., 2019; Jadhav et al., 2012; Petersen and Buzsáki, 2020; Robbe and Buzsáki, 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: PFC cells phase-lock and phase-precess to hippocampal theta oscillations.
source: previous studies have shown that PFC cells phase-lock and phase-precess (i.e. spikes of a cell occur at progressively earlier theta phases as an animal move through its spatial field) to hippocampal theta oscillations (Jadhav et al., 2016; Jones and Wilson, 2005a; Siapas et al., 2005; Sigurdsson et al., 2010)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Theta-frequency synchrony and coherent spatial coding between the hippocampus and PFC is prominent during memory-guided navigation.
source: further, theta-frequency synchrony and coherent spatial coding between the hippocampus and PFC is prominent during memory-guided navigation (Benchenane et al., 2010; Gordon, 2011; Hasz and Redish, 2020; Jones and Wilson, 2005b; Sigurdsson et al., 2010; Zielinski et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: CA1 replay sequences underlie deliberation between actual and alternative choices.
source: Previously, we have reported that CA1 replay sequences, similar to its theta sequences reported here, underlie deliberation between actual and alternative choices
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous study by the authors.

claim: CA1-PFC reactivation represents actual choice for current trials.
source: whereas CA1-PFC reactivation represents actual choice for current trials (Shin et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous study by the authors.

claim: Disrupting awake SWRs leads to increase in errors in the spatial working memory task.
source: and disrupting awake SWRs leads to increase in errors in the spatial working memory task (Fernández-Ruiz et al., 2019; Jadhav et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: SWR-reactivation in the hippocampus is less coordinated prior to incorrect versus correct trials.
source: Previous studies have shown that SWR-reactivation in the hippocampus is less coordinated prior to incorrect versus correct trials (Shin et al., 2019; Singer et al., 2013)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: There is a relationship between reverse and forward CA1-PFC replay with past and future trajectories, respectively.
source: In addition, we have previously shown a relationship between reverse and forward CA1-PFC replay with past and future trajectories, respectively (Shin et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous study by the authors.

claim: Degradation of theta sequences results in impaired sequential activation during sleep replay in the hippocampus.
source: Finally, there is evidence that degradation of theta sequences results in impaired sequential activation during sleep replay in the hippocampus (Drieu et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Theta oscillation cycles comprise cognitive computation units, corresponding to segregation of cell assemblies that represent different spatial experiences.
source: previous studies have shown that theta oscillation cycles comprise cognitive computation units, corresponding to segregation of cell assemblies that represent different spatial experiences (Brandon et al., 2013; Geisler et al., 2007; Gupta et al., 2012; Jezek et al., 2011)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Cortical neurons are sensitive to temporally organized inputs from the hippocampus.
source: It has been shown that cortical neurons are sensitive to temporally organized inputs from the hippocampus (Branco et al., 2010; Siapas et al., 2005; Sigurdsson et al., 2010)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Pharmacological disruption of prefrontal activity results in impaired theta sequences in the hippocampus.
source: and pharmacological disruption of prefrontal activity results in impaired theta sequences in the hippocampus (Schmidt et al., 2019)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Pharmacological disruption of prefrontal activity results in impaired performance in the W-track task.
source: as well as impaired performance in the W-track task (Maharjan et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Behavioral-state-dependent prefrontal-hippocampal interactions during theta oscillations can potentially be mediated through connections with entorhinal cortex.
source: Behavioral-state-dependent prefrontal-hippocampal interactions during theta oscillations can potentially also be mediated through connections with entorhinal cortex (Fernández-Ruiz et al., 2017)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Behavioral-state-dependent prefrontal-hippocampal interactions during theta oscillations can potentially be mediated through connections with nucleus reuniens.
source: nucleus reuniens (Ito et al., 2015)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: The mechanism of using internally generated sequences to simulate future scenarios has been used as a key feature that improves performance of model-based learning computations.
source: Notably, the mechanism of using internally generated sequences to simulate future scenarios has been used as a key feature that improves performance of model-based learning computations (Daw and Dayan, 2014; Mattar and Daw, 2018; Pezzulo et al., 2019; Pezzulo et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Theta timescale mechanisms in CA1 can represent possible future paths and possible directions of motion on a moment-to-moment basis.
source: In agreement with this idea, a recent study has shown that theta timescale mechanisms in CA1 can not only represent possible future paths, but also possible directions of motion on a moment-to-moment basis (Kay et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Representation of past locations within theta cycles has been recently reported.
source: Representation of past locations within theta cycles has also been recently reported (Wang et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Theta sequences in CA1 and PFC are nested within behavioral-timescale sequences during navigation.
source: These transient theta sequences in CA1 and PFC were nested within behavioral-timescale sequences during navigation.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by data in Figure 1C and Figure 2.

claim: Theta sequences retain representations of choice options to support vicarious memory recall and deliberative decision-making.
source: However, in contrast to trajectory-dependent firing sequences at the behavioral-timescale, theta sequences retain representations of choice options to support vicarious memory recall and deliberative decision-making
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by data in Figure 6.

claim: Fast replay sequences are involved in decision priming prior to onset of navigation.
source: and function in a complementary manner with fast replay sequences involved in decision priming prior to onset of navigation
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 7.

claim: Coherent CA1-PFC replay of future trajectories prior to navigation onset primes the chosen destination in this memory-guided decision-making task.
source: our current findings provide definitive evidence that coherent CA1-PFC replay of future trajectories prior to navigation onset primes the chosen destination in this memory-guided decision-making task
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 7.

claim: Errors in CA1-PFC replay predict incorrect decisions.
source: and errors in CA1-PFC replay predict incorrect decisions.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 7F.

claim: Choice-specific representations of both theta and replay sequences depend on choice encoding through trajectory preferred firing of behavioral sequences.
source: Choice-specific representations of both theta and replay sequences depend on choice encoding through trajectory preferred firing of behavioral sequences.
evidence: This is an inference based on the data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Trajectory-selective neurons showed an extended tail of their spatial fields, which likely contributes to trajectory-modulated look-ahead of theta sequences.
source: Furthermore, trajectory-selective neurons showed an extended tail of their spatial fields, which is inherently a behavioral-timescale characteristic, and likely contributes to trajectory-modulated look-ahead of theta sequences.
evidence: This is an inference based on the data presented in Figure 4.

claim: It is the interactions among multi-timescale activity patterns that potentially govern decision-making.
source: Thus, it is the interactions among these multi-timescale activity patterns that potentially govern decision-making.
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion based on the findings of the study.

claim: Transient LFP oscillations may be informative signatures of fast evolving cell assemblies that bear on decision-making processes.
source: Together, these results suggest the possibility of transient LFP oscillations as informative signatures of fast evolving cell assemblies that bear on decision-making processes
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion based on the findings of the study and previous literature.

claim: The cooperative behavioral- and cognitive-timescale mechanisms may reflect a general organizing principle of neural dynamics underlying decision-making.
source: and the cooperative behavioral- and cognitive-timescale mechanisms described here may reflect a general organizing principle of neural dynamics underlying decision-making.
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion based on the findings of the study.

claim: Nine adult male Long-Evans rats (450–550 g, 4–6 months) were used in this study.
source: Nine adult male Long-Evans rats (450–550 g, 4–6 months) were used in this study.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental subjects.

source: All procedures were approved by the Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee at the Brandeis University and conformed to US National Institutes of Health guidelines.
evidence: This is a statement about ethical approval.

source: Data from six subjects have been reported in an earlier study (Shin et al., 2019).
